title: North-South inequalities
subtitle: A two-speed world
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: The richest 10% on the planet capture more than half of global income. However, extreme poverty has been divided by four in thirty years.

hero.hook: An American earns in an hour what a resident of Niger earns in a whole day of work.

blocks.text: The gap between rich and poor countries remains one of the most striking facts in the world today. Globalization promised a rapprochement in living standards, but wealth gaps remain immense between nations.

However, recent history is not only gloomy: extreme poverty has declined faster than ever in thirty years. This course explores the roots of these inequalities, and the reasons for this strange paradox.

The **** richest 10% of the world's population capture more than 52% of global income. The poorest 50% must share only 8% of the pie. This concentration of wealth has never been greater in human history.

This divide is also seen in life expectancy: it reaches 83 years in Japan, but falls to 55 years in the Central African Republic. These gaps are not due to chance: they come from very unequal access to drinking water, food and health care.
An inhabitant of the United States earns on average, in one hour of work, as much as an inhabitant of Niger in an entire day.

To understand these differences, we must go back to colonization. European powers organized many southern territories as suppliers of raw materials (coffee, cocoa, cotton), slowing their own industrialization to protect their own factories.

blocks.caption: The wealth gaps between North and South remain among the widest on the planet.

blocks.text: This logic continues today through the [[terms of trade]]: countries of the South often sell raw materials whose price varies greatly, while they buy manufactured products whose price only increases. Added to this is the weight of the debt: repaying interest sometimes takes up more space in a national budget than education or health.

However, the last thirty years have seen a spectacular decline in absolute poverty, which affected 36% of the world population in 1990, compared to less than 10% before 2020. This progress comes mainly from the meteoric growth of China and India.

This progress has a hidden side: this is what the [[“elephant curve”]] of economist Branko Milanovic shows. The Asian middle classes have seen their incomes explode, but the working classes in rich countries have stagnated, faced with global competition. Reducing inequalities between countries has therefore not prevented new tensions even within rich countries.

The future of North-South inequalities now depends on the climate. The countries of the South, historically the least responsible for greenhouse gas emissions, are nevertheless the most exposed to droughts, floods and rising water levels.

To reduce these gaps sustainably, the international community is exploring new avenues:  targeted on the energy transition, or cancellation of the debt of the most fragile countries. As long as the wealth of the richest grows faster than that of the poorest, tensions will remain high. [[official development assistance]]

The richest 10% of the world capture more than half of global income, but extreme poverty has declined faster than ever in thirty years thanks to the rise of China and India. The next big challenge in this North-South divide will be climate.
